title: MYP Design Criteria A to D Explained
summary: MYP Design criteria A to D explained in plain language, with high-band expectations, feedback tips, and practical advice for students and parents.
body_markdown:
A teacher writes, “Your product is promising, but the evidence behind your decisions needs more depth.” The student sees criticism. The teacher sees directions.


That difference matters in MYP Design. The subject is not assessed only on whether the final product looks impressive or works perfectly. The **MYP Design criteria** assess the entire design cycle: understanding a problem, developing ideas, creating a solution, and evaluating its success.


There are four criteria, each generally assessed on an achievement scale from 0-8. The precise wording and level of scaffolding vary by MYP year, so students should always use the task-specific rubric supplied by their teacher. Still, the underlying journey remains recognizable across the programme.


Students and parents can explore the wider programme through the[RevisionDojo MYP resource hub](https://www.revisiondojo.com/myp) and see how Design fits within the[eight MYP subject groups](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/what-are-myp-subject-groups) .


### The MYP Design criteria at a glance


The four criteria follow a logical sequence:


- **Criterion A: Inquiring and analysing** asks whether the student understands the problem and has researched it intelligently.
- **Criterion B: Developing ideas** asks whether the student has established success criteria, explored possible solutions, and planned a chosen design.
- **Criterion C: Creating the solution** assesses planning, technical execution, functionality, and justified changes.
- **Criterion D: Evaluating** asks whether the student tested the solution, judged it against the design specification, proposed improvements, and considered its impact.


A useful way to remember the sequence is: **investigate, imagine, make, evaluate** . These are connected stages, not four unrelated assignments.


### MYP Design criterion A: Inquiring and analysing


Imagine the student rereads the teacher’s first comment: “You described the problem, but you did not justify why your client needs a solution.”


That single sentence captures a common weakness in **MYP Design criterion A** . A student may announce, “My client needs a desk organiser,” but never investigate who the client is, what causes the difficulty, or why existing solutions are unsuitable.
